claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by the degree of atomic mixing and alloy-phase uniformity.
Greater atomic-level homogeneity improves catalytic activity relative to phase-segregated or core–shell nanoparticles of the same composition.
Greater atomic-level homogeneity improves catalytic stability relative to phase-segregated or core–shell nanoparticles of the same composition.
Random mixing of constituent noble metals produces synergistic electronic effects.
Random atomic mixing maximizes active-site diversity.
Homogeneous atomic mixing tunes the d-band structure through electronic interactions among the constituent metals.
The electronic interactions and resulting diversity of active sites enhance catalytic activity and stability.
Phase-segregated or core–shell structures limit electronic synergy and active-site diversity.
Homogeneous HEA nanoparticles are expected to exhibit more than a 30% improvement in catalytic activity over phase-segregated or core–shell counterparts.
Homogeneous HEA nanoparticles are expected to resist dissolution or aggregation better than phase-segregated or core–shell counterparts.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm that contain at least three noble metals and are synthesized under conditions permitting atomic mixing.
The hypothesis may not apply to larger particles, non-noble-metal systems, or HEAs with significant compositional gradients.
Atomic mixing is assumed to be the dominant determinant of performance when composition and particle size are controlled.
Surface structure and ligand effects may also contribute to catalytic performance.
